newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Oil climbs on Nigeria, Iraq, but tone weak.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Oil climbs on Nigeria, Iraq, but tone weak.

text.p: World oil prices firmed on Tuesday for the third successive day on the possibility of lower oil exports from Nigeria and heightened tension between Iraq and the United States.
But the underlying market tone remained weak and some dealers predicted little chance of further gains.

"I'm not very impressed by this market. The helicopters are pretty insignificant and Nigeria is a perennial problem," said Nigel Saperia, managing director of the oil division at Bankers Trust International in London.
"We're looking at the top of this little move give or take 10 cents," he said.
Bellwether London Brent crude futures for June delivery were up 19 cents a barrel at $18.53 at 1125 GMT, well above the nine-month low of $17.54 hit about three weeks ago.
But the downdraft in oil prices has been severe since January when prices touched nearly $25 a barrel. Last year the average for Brent was $20.32 a barrel.

Nigerian exports were threatened with delays but cancellations are not expected, said operators Shell on Tuesday. Royal Dutch Shell Group's Nigerian unit said earlier on Tuesday it had declared force majeure on export of Bonny crude oil because of a strike by contractors that handle the berthing and loading of tankers.
Meanwhile, Iraqi helicopters arrived safely at Iraq's southern border with Saudi Arabia to pick up Moslem pilgrims, the official Iraqi News Agency (INA) said on Tuesday.

The White House on Monday urged Iraq to reconsider, saying it would "respond appropriately" to any such flights. U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen said Iraq could not flout no-fly rules by arbitrarily sending helicopters to pick up the pilgrims, but it might be eligible for a humanitarian exemption allowing the flights if it followed proper procedure.

Prices also found support this week from news that OPEC's president Libyan Oil Minister Abdalla el-Badri had called on Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries' members to restrain output to help support sagging crude prices.
"The president has been calling and asking members to exercise restraint," OPEC Secretary-General Rilwanu Lukman told Reuters on the sidelines of an industry conference here.
"We will have to wait and see," whether member countries would respond, Lukman added.

OPEC output, estimated in a Reuters survey at 26.90 million barrels per day in March, has risen by about a million barrels per day (bpd) in the past year and is approaching two million bpd above the group's official 25.03 million ceiling.
Unseasonably cold weather in the key heating oil market of the Northeast United States has also been helping support prices, traders said.
Although more normal temperatures are expected soon, a seasonal pick up in gasoline demand is expected in the United States.
